extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts legal rules and practical standards for patentability, claim construction, interference, infringement, and remedies from a judge's decision and accompanying index in a patent-law treatise. Useful for evaluating whether subject matter is patentable, whether claims interfere, and procedural/ evidentiary requirements in patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patentability (new effect from old materials)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination or arrangement of old materials, when, in consequence thereof a new effect is produced, may be the subject of a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This effect may be producing a new article, or making an old one better or cheaper; the grant is for the new and useful compound or thing produced by combining known things with something newly invented to produce an effect never before attained. (Quoted from Mr. Godson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Old elements plus new matter can form patentable combination
rubrics_metrics.description: The old matter may not, in itself, be patentable, but joined to the new matter, a combination may be formed which may be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An inventor need not take separate patents for each new patentable matter; he may claim the limited use of the new matters in combination rather than exclusive use for every purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form and structure as identity of machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: When the application is for a patent for a combination of machinery and materials, form and structure become substance; they are of the essence of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitting that two instruments differ 'in form and structure' is prima facie evidence that there is no interference between them; differences in form/structure that enable better/easier/cheaper/faster operation support distinct patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent cannot be for a principle, application of a principle, or an effect
rubrics_metrics.description: There cannot be a patent for a principle; nor for the application of a principle; nor for an effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two persons may use the same principle and produce the same effect by different means without interference; each may obtain a patent for his own means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable improvement is not an interference
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentable improvement of an existing device does not constitute an interference with an older patent for a different form/structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If form/structure differences enable improved performance or economy, the improvement inventor may obtain a patent distinct from prior devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interference decided on patentable matter, not non-patentable elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Where several elemental features are old and not now patentable, an interference must concern the matter that is now patentable (e.g., a new combination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims that cover only old unpatentable elements do not create interference; only overlapping claims to patentable matter are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of difference shifts burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: An admission that one party's instrument is 'a very different thing, in its form and structure' from another is prima facie evidence that there is no interference and throws the burden of proof on the other side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts rely on differences in specifications, drawings, and models to perceive substantive distinctions between inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to monopoly tied to invented principle of operation
rubrics_metrics.description: A person can monopolize the use of principles of operation which he may have invented or discovered (e.g., use of galvanic power to mark signs on chemically prepared paper by a single circuit), but not the raw elements like air/fire/water themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The right attaches to the method/principle and its specific application; mere general resources remain public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority (first inventor) vs. differences in means
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if two applicants use the same power and subject, where the effect is produced by means so different as to prevent interference, the question of priority of invention does not arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such cases fall under the statutory section for distinct inventions (referred to here as the 7th section) rather than interference under priority rules (8th section).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment of invention destroys right to a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment of an invention destroys the right to a patent and ought to be clearly proved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abandonment can be shown by acquiescence in public use or sale; it is not established merely by making for experiment; conclusive evidence may be required; intention and duration considerations discussed (see multiple cross-references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment not proven by experimental practice
rubrics_metrics.description: A patentee's experimental practice does not constitute abandonment of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Making for experiment, or experimental use by the inventor, does not necessarily bar patent rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account of profits as equitable remedy in lieu of injunction
rubrics_metrics.description: An account of profits may be ordered in lieu of granting an injunction, subject to principles guiding equitable relief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ordered, it extends to all the articles made; the court determines on what principle profits are awarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action at law requirements for infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.description: A declaration in an action at law should show that plaintiff was first inventor, that the subject-matter was new and useful, the substance of the grant, the value of the patent, the breach by defendant, and damages sustained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pleadings and defenses are governed by statute; assignees and grantees may bring suits; omission in declaration may be cured by verdict; proof of recording assignment may be admitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defenses in infringement suits under general issue
rubrics_metrics.description: Defenses include that the defendant never did the act complained of; that the plaintiff was not entitled to a patent; lack of good title; patent not duly issued; subject not patentable; lack of utility; unintelligible specification; concealment or addition in specification; want of novelty; prior dedication to the public; surreptitious procurement; unreasonable withholding from the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some defenses require notice; statutory provisions define practice; these defenses may be pleaded under the general issue or specially as appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amendments and disclaimers in specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Amendments of specifications are allowed by statute and may be made by disclaimer; disclaimers become part of the specifications and are to be recorded in the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects include how pending actions are affected and implications for costs; disclaimers may be used to cure defects in specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant formalities for patent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Application for patent must be made in writing (by petition), accompanied with specifications, and the applicant must make prescribed oaths and pay required fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications may be withdrawn; caveats may be filed; applicants may appeal Commissioner decisions; aliens and administrators have particular rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat filing and confidentiality
rubrics_metrics.description: A caveat may be filed in the confidential archives of the Patent Office; aliens may file caveats under certain conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a caveat preserves certain rights and is governed by statutory fees and procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty and prior art: elements not patentable if previously known
rubrics_metrics.description: If elements such as a single telegraphic circuit, chemically prepared paper, or the signs themselves have been long known or previously patented, claims to them individually are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patentable claims must rest on new matter or new combinations producing new effects; prior patents/printed publications or secret archives may defeat novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of matter patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition of matter is patentable when meeting statutory tests; includes criteria for novelty and infringement of compositions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cross-references tests of novelty and how patent for composition is infringed; descriptions and how to claim compositions are treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment vitiates specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealment in specifications can vitiate the patent or be a ground for defense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concealment or improper addition in specifications may require notice in pleadings and can lead to invalidation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction (interpretation) of patents by courts
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of a patent is the province of the court (questions of law), although juries may decide factual matters; courts should be liberal in construction and guided by principles in specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts decide extent of claim, sufficiency of invention, whether patent void as against public policy, and how to receive evidence of invention; principles guide how far courts may receive evidence to explain specifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Copying as infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: A copy constitutes an infringement when it reproduces the patented invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases and statutory references treat copying as actionable; the page references tests and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable relief and injunction principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts of equity may restrain infringements by injunctions; the granting of injunctions is discretionary and guided by general equitable principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requirements include affidavits, notice to defendant, that injunctions are not granted ex parte, and considerations whether patentee must first establish the right at law; rules from Lord Eldon and adopted practice inform when injunctions issue, dissolve, or are modified; account of profits sometimes substituted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards in patent litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Two kinds of evidence in patent causes: title/priority evidence and evidence of infringement/sufficiency; competent evidence to show granting of patent, prima facie novelty, negative evidence, and expert testimony on sufficiency of specifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissibility and weight depend on subject matter; who is a competent expert varies (persons of ordinary skill vs thoroughly scientific persons); copies of records under seal may be evidence; courts determine sufficiency of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert testimony and competence
rubrics_metrics.description: Experts may be persons of ordinary skill or thoroughly scientific persons depending on the subject-matter; courts determine when experts are admissible and competent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nature of the evidence and scope of expert testimony depend on the invention's technical complexity; expert evidence commonly used to explain specifications and testify to identity or infringement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments do not necessarily constitute invention or abandonment
rubrics_metrics.description: Unsuccessful experiments do not prevent subsequent invention; experimental practice by the inventor is distinct from abandonment and generally does not defeat patent rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Antecedent experiments by others may be used by inventor; unsuccessful experiments are treated differently from public dedication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of patent (statutory relief)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extensions may be granted under statute for limited times (cannot exceed seven years in referenced statute); the Commissioner has authority to decide extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrator/executor may apply; extensions generally do not enure to assignees; fees and procedures apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignees' rights and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: Assignees of patents have rights in case of extension or renewal, may amend specifications, and may bring suits for infringement (sometimes with special rules for assignment for particular districts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments should be recorded; assignees' abilities to amend, sue in equity, or recover depend on statutes and recording practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description and drawings as part of specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Descriptions of machines may be partly in writing and partly by drawings; drawings form part of the specifications and should accompany them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whether drawings need to be to scale, duplicates required, and how drawings are used in claim construction are covered; drawings and models may be required and classified by the Commissioner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Designs and art-works: subject-matter limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Designs may be subject of a patent under certain conditions; fine arts generally not patentable; tradesmen's marks may be included in designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page cross-references statutory provisions and tests for when designs are patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclaimer effects on pending suits and costs
rubrics_metrics.description: A statutory disclaimer may be recorded and taken as part of specifications; it affects pending litigation and may influence award of costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclaimers are a mechanism to limit claims and cure defects, but have procedural and substantive consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior dedication/public use as defense
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior dedication of the invention to the public (or prior public use) is a defense to patent validity and an equitable defense in injunction suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior dedication must be shown; it affects equitable relief and may bar injunctions; courts treat such defenses specially in equity practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages in infringement actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Damages rules: actual damages, potential trebling by court, nominal damages, and possibility to include counsel fees and witness expenses; damages may be awarded for infringement after destruction of Patent Office records and subject to rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess damages on proof of value and breach; remedies in equity (account of profits) and law (damages) interact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity in infringement analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity in machinery, manufacture, or application of a principle is the key issue in infringement: what constitutes 'identity' depends on factual and technical comparison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two kinds of evidence apply to identity questions; courts use expert evidence and comparison of specifications/drawings/models to determine identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Colorable variations and immaterial changes not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Colorable variations or mere changes of former proportions (when unimportant) are not patentable; materiality of a change is determined by whether it produces utility or substantial improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility is a test of invention; merely omitting a usual ingredient or insignificant proportions typically do not suffice for patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedure for affidavits in equity (injunction) applications
rubrics_metrics.description: An affidavit in support of motion for an injunction should be provided and may be read in support of title; it is part of equitable practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Affidavits must be sworn and typically accompany applications for preliminary equitable relief; they may be read in subsequent proceedings on title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commissioner of Patents duties and powers
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commissioner signs patents, examines inventions, decides on interfering applications, may correct mistakes, make classifications of models, appoint clerks/examiners, and decide extensions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commissioner's opinions are not always re-examinable; applications may appeal Commissioner decisions to courts; statutory procedures govern office administration.
